lessons.title: Combining Factors: Building Your First Multi-Signal Stat Arb Sleeve

children.text: Lesson 26 gave three distinct factors. Lesson 27 cleaned the overlap between two of them. This lesson does the last step: turning several factor scores per stock into one composite score, and using that composite score to build an actual long-short portfolio, the same logic this course has used for a single pair, now applied across several stocks at once.

body.text: Combining factors means turning several scores per stock into one composite score, then treating that composite exactly like this course's z-score all along: rank everything, go long the extreme winners, short the extreme losers, sized to keep the overall book roughly market-neutral.

children.text: The Simplest Way to Combine: An Equal-Weighted Average

The standard, transparent default is to average each stock's standardized scores across factors, ideally using orthogonalized versions where meaningful overlap exists, as Lesson 27 did for momentum. More sophisticated approaches exist, weighting factors by how much a desk trusts each one, or by their own historical risk and return characteristics through some form of optimization, but the equal-weighted average is a reasonable, honest starting point and the one this lesson uses.
Worked Example: Combining Three Factors for Six Stocks

Returning to Lesson 27's six stocks, add a third factor, an illustrative mean-reversion score, this course's own specialty. Checking it against Value first, its correlation comes out around -0.17, low enough that it can reasonably be combined directly for this example without a separate orthogonalization step, though a fully rigorous pipeline would check every pair of factors, not just the ones that happen to look correlated at a glance.

body.caption: Three factor scores for six illustrative stocks

body.code:
import numpy as np

value = np.array([1.5, 0.8, -0.3, -1.2, 0.4, -0.6])
clean_momentum = np.array([-0.31, -0.38, -0.09, 0.12, 1.28, -0.62])
mean_reversion = np.array([-0.5, 0.9, 0.3, -0.7, -1.5, 1.8])

composite = (value + clean_momentum + mean_reversion) / 3
print(np.round(composite, 2))
# [ 0.23  0.44 -0.03 -0.59  0.06  0.19]
body.caption: An equal-weighted composite score across the three factors

children.text: From Composite Score to a Portfolio

Rank the six stocks by their composite score, go long the highest scorers, short the lowest, and leave the middle untraded, exactly the entry logic Lesson 14 used for a single pair's z-score, now applied across a whole ranked list.

body.caption: From composite score to a long-short sleeve

children.text: With two long positions (B and A) and two short positions (C and D), the simplest sizing approach splits equal rupee value across each side, say ₹2.5 lakh in each of B and A, and ₹2.5 lakh short in each of C and D, for a dollar-neutral ₹10 lakh book. Lesson 15 already showed why equal rupee value is not the same as genuine market-neutrality for a single pair, and the same logic scales up here: a properly hedged book would weight each position by its own beta to the market, so the portfolio's overall net market exposure, not just its rupee totals, comes out close to zero. Getting this exactly right for a multi-stock book is more involved than for a single pair, and is typically handled with the kind of portfolio-level optimization covered in dedicated portfolio construction courses, beyond this course's pairs-and-factors scope.

body.title: Compute a composite score
body.prompt: A seventh stock has a Value score of 0.6, a clean momentum score of -0.4, and a mean-reversion score of 1.0. What is its equal-weighted composite score?

body.title: Why not just use the raw momentum score?
body.question: When building this lesson's composite score, why was Lesson 27's orthogonalized (clean) momentum score used instead of the original raw momentum score?
options: Raw scores cannot be averaged mathematically
Using the clean momentum score avoids double-counting the overlap between momentum and value that Lesson 27 identified and removed
Clean scores are always higher than raw scores
It makes no difference which version is used
body.explanation: Lesson 27 showed that raw momentum and value scores were correlated in this sample. Using the clean, orthogonalized momentum score in the composite ensures the combination reflects three genuinely distinct pieces of information, rather than counting the value-momentum overlap twice under two different names.

cards.definition: A single combined score per stock, typically an average of several individual (ideally orthogonalized) factor scores, used to rank stocks for a multi-factor strategy.
A long-short portfolio built from ranking stocks by a composite factor score and taking positions in the extremes, generalizing a single pair's long-short structure to many stocks.

points: The simplest way to combine multiple factor scores is an equal-weighted average, ideally using orthogonalized versions of each factor (Lesson 27) so the combination doesn't double-count shared overlap.

In this lesson's worked example, combining value, clean momentum, and mean-reversion scores for six stocks produced a composite ranking, leading to a long position in the two highest scorers and a short position in the two lowest, with the middle two stocks left untraded.

Building a portfolio from a composite score is the same logic this course has used throughout: rank, act on the extremes, size to stay roughly neutral, just applied across several stocks rather than one pair.

Equal rupee value on the long and short sides is a simple default, but genuine market-neutrality at the portfolio level ideally weights each position by its own beta, generalizing Lesson 15's dollar-neutral-vs-hedge-ratio distinction to a multi-stock book.

More sophisticated ways to combine and weight factors, and to properly beta-neutralize a multi-stock portfolio, exist and are used by professional desks, but are beyond this course's pairs-and-factors scope.
